Getting Started with glmap

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

Why glmap?

🌱 ELI5 (Plain-English Mental Model)
  • One-Line Magic: Give glmap() almost any spatial object in R (points, polygons, or a terra raster grid) and it figures out how to draw it automatically.
  • No More Color Functions: In leaflet, you had to build a separate pal <- colorNumeric(…) function and manually wire up a legend. In glmap, you just write color = ~my_column, palette = “viridis” and both the colors and legend appear automatically.
  • Instant Raster Sliders: When you plot a terra raster, glmap sends the actual numbers to your graphics card. You can flip between palettes or turn on 3D hillshade shadows in the browser in 0 milliseconds without waiting for R!

⚙️ Technical Mode (C++17 + WebGL2 Pipeline)
Traditional R mapping packages built on Leaflet.js serialize spatial objects into GeoJSON text inside HTML and draw features using DOM/SVG/2D Canvas. When your dataset reaches 100,000 to 1,000,000+ features or uses high-resolution terra rasters, R spends tens of seconds converting coordinates to text and the browser tab freezes.

glmap eliminates the JSON and DOM bottlenecks entirely via C++17 GLMP/GLMR binary buffers, C++ mapbox/earcut.h polygon triangulation, and WebGL2 instanced SDF & RGBA32F floating-point raster fragment shaders.

1. Instant One-Line Exploration

glmap() inspects your input (sf, sfc, terra::SpatRaster, terra::SpatVector, wk::xy, nanoarrow, data.frame, or crosstalk::SharedData) and automatically chooses the right GPU layer:

library(glmap)

# Generate synthetic benchmark data
bench <- gl_benchmark_data(n_points = 15000L, n_polygons = 600L)

# Instant GPU map of 15,000 points
glmap(bench$points_df, color = ~intensity, palette = "turbo", radius = 3.5, height = "420px")

# Instant GPU map of a Float32 DEM raster with real-time hillshading
glmap(bench$raster_mat, palette = "terrain", hillshade = TRUE, height = "420px")

2. Building Multi-Layer GPU Maps with Pipes (|>)

Use glmap() with add_raster(), add_polygons(), add_lines(), add_points(), add_hexbin(), add_heatmap(), and add_labels():

glmap(basemap = "dark", height = "460px") |>
  add_raster(
    bench$raster_mat,
    palette = "terrain",
    hillshade = TRUE,
    opacity = 0.65,
    group = "Terrain DEM (Float32)"
  ) |>
  add_polygons(
    bench$polygons_sf,
    fill_color = ~elevation,
    palette = "viridis",
    fill_opacity = 0.65,
    group = "Polygons (C++ Earcut)"
  ) |>
  add_hexbin(
    bench$points_df,
    hex_radius = 0.035,
    palette = "plasma",
    opacity = 0.75,
    group = "Hexbins (C++ 64-bit Hash)"
  ) |>
  add_points(
    bench$points_df,
    color = ~intensity,
    palette = "turbo",
    radius = 3.0,
    opacity = 0.85,
    group = "Points (WebGL2 SDF)"
  ) |>
  use_plugin("export_png")

3. Handling 1M–10M+ Features with In-Memory C++ Spatial Indexing or DuckDB

For massive datasets in interactive R or Shiny sessions, enable dynamic_viewport = TRUE, transport = "server", or add_duckdb(). glmap builds an in-memory C++ spatial index (gl_spatial_index()) or queries DuckDB to stream only the features inside the current viewport with automatic Level-of-Detail (LOD) stride sampling:

# Generate 100,000 points and render via inline compressed GLMP binary buffer
big_df <- data.frame(
  lon = runif(100000, -75, -71),
  lat = runif(100000, 45, 48),
  val = rnorm(100000)
)

glmap(basemap = "dark", height = "440px") |>
  add_points(
    big_df,
    color = ~val,
    palette = "viridis",
    radius = 2.5,
    opacity = 0.8
  )

Tip for 1M–10M+ features in interactive R or Shiny sessions: Pass transport = "server" or dynamic_viewport = TRUE to stream viewport slices over the local httpuv binary server (127.0.0.1) instead of embedding them inline in the HTML file.
